items.name: SSRIs
hx: Block serotonin 5-HT2A receptors
They block the reuptake transporter (SERT), raising synaptic serotonin.
Stimulate serotonin release (5-HT1A)
They block reuptake.
Block dopamine reuptake (DAT)
That's bupropion-like; SSRIs block SERT.
items.sewhy: Serotonin in the gut (nausea), sexual pathways (dysfunction) and platelets (less serotonin uptake, more bleeding); SIADH lowers sodium in older people, and early activation can raise suicidality in under-25s.

x: The risk is switching into mania.
No; it can trigger a manic switch.

ci.c: With MAOIs or within 2 weeks (5 for fluoxetine)
x: That comes from anaesthetic agents; SSRIs with MAOIs cause serotonin syndrome.
NSAIDs don't add serotonin; the risk is GI bleeding.
↓ anticoagulant effect; raise the warfarin dose
Review within 6 months for weight gain
Under-25s need review within a week for suicidal thoughts.
They can be used, with early review for suicidality.
Review within 1 week for serotonin syndrome
The early review is for suicidality.

items.name: SNRIs
hx: Block serotonin and dopamine reuptake
SNRIs block serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake.
Block serotonin and noradrenaline receptors
They block reuptake, raising levels; blocking receptors would do the opposite.
Release serotonin and noradrenaline from vesicles
That's amphetamine-like; SNRIs block reuptake.
items.sewhy: As well as serotonergic effects, raising noradrenaline increases BP and sweating; short half-lives (venlafaxine) cause severe discontinuation symptoms.

x: No; the noradrenergic effect raises BP.
That's antipsychotics; SNRIs with MAOIs cause serotonin syndrome.
Venlafaxine is pro-arrhythmic and raises BP.
Not the reason; pro-arrhythmic and raises BP.

items.name: Mirtazapine
items.how: α2 antagonist (↑ NA and 5-HT release) and H1 antagonist
hx: α2 agonist (↓ NA release) and H1 agonist
It blocks α2 autoreceptors, increasing release, and blocks H1.
α1 antagonist (↓ BP) and D2 antagonist
It blocks α2 (and H1).
5-HT3 agonist (↑ 5-HT release) and H2 antagonist
It's an α2 antagonist and H1 antagonist.
items.sewhy: It blocks H1 receptors strongly (sedation, appetite, weight gain), most noticeably at low doses.

x: Rare with mirtazapine alone; with MAOIs the risk is serotonin syndrome.
Possible, but the concern here is weight gain.

items.name: Tricyclic antidepressants
items.how: Block serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake; also antimuscarinic, antihistamine, α1-blocking
hx: Block serotonin and dopamine reuptake; also cholinergic, antihistamine, β1-blocking
They block 5-HT/NA reuptake and are antimuscarinic and α1-blocking.
Block serotonin and noradrenaline release; also muscarinic and α1 agonists
They block reuptake, and block (not stimulate) muscarinic and α1 receptors.
Open K⁺ channels in neurons; also antimuscarinic and antihistamine
Their antidepressant action is 5-HT/NA reuptake block.
se: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision
items.sewhy: TCAs block muscarinic (dry mouth, constipation, retention), H1 (sedation, weight gain), α1 (postural hypotension) and cardiac sodium channels (QRS widening, arrhythmias), which is why overdose is lethal.

x: They're pro-arrhythmic (and lower BP through α1 block).
They speed the heart and are pro-arrhythmic.
They block Na⁺ channels, widening QRS.
Ca²⁺-channel block slows the SA node
The key effect is Na⁺-channel block (wide QRS).
Possible in overdose, but the concern in mania is a manic switch.
TCAs are very dangerous in overdose.
TCA overdose causes seizures and broad-QRS arrhythmias.
TCAs cause sedation, postural hypotension and confusion, so falls.

items.name: MAOIs
items.how: Block monoamine oxidase → ↑ serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine
hx: Activate monoamine oxidase → ↓ serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine
They block MAO, raising monoamines.
Block COMT → ↑ dopamine only
That's entacapone; MAOIs block monoamine oxidase.
Block monoamine oxidase → ↑ acetylcholine and GABA
MAO breaks down monoamines (5-HT, NA, dopamine).
items.sewhy: MAO normally breaks down tyramine from food; blocking it lets tyramine release noradrenaline, causing a hypertensive crisis.

ci.c: With SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans or tramadol
x: That's antipsychotics; here it's serotonin syndrome.
Tyramine releases noradrenaline, causing a hypertensive crisis.
Tyramine blocks the MAOI → depression relapse
No; unmetabolised tyramine causes a hypertensive crisis.
The culprit is tyramine (noradrenaline release → hypertensive crisis).

items.name: Lithium
items.how: Not fully understood (inositol depletion, GSK-3 inhibition); narrow range 0.4–1.0 mmol/L
hx: Blocks D2 receptors; wide range 2–4 mmol/L
Its mechanism isn't fully known (inositol depletion, GSK-3), and the range is narrow: 0.4–1.0.
Enhances GABA-A receptors; narrow range 1.5–3.0 mmol/L
The target is 0.4–1.0 mmol/L; above 1.5 is toxic.
Blocks serotonin reuptake; no level monitoring needed
Lithium needs regular levels (0.4–1.0 mmol/L).
se: Toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting, seizures
items.sewhy: Lithium blocks ADH action in the collecting duct (polyuria, nephrogenic DI) and thyroid hormone release (hypothyroidism); the therapeutic range is narrow, so dehydration or interacting drugs cause toxicity.

x: Lithium is cleared by the kidneys.
Lithium affects cardiac conduction (sinus node, Brugada).

ci.why: Sodium depletion → more lithium reabsorbed → toxicity
x: Sodium excess → more lithium excreted → relapse
Low sodium makes the kidney hold lithium → toxicity.
Cortisol deficiency → lithium can't be absorbed
No; sodium depletion raises lithium reabsorption.
Sodium depletion → less lithium reabsorbed → relapse
More lithium is reabsorbed with sodium, raising levels.
Lithium is linked to Ebstein's anomaly (tricuspid valve).

items.name: Antipsychotics
hx: Stimulate D2 receptors (atypicals also stimulate 5-HT2A)
They block D2 (and atypicals block 5-HT2A).
Block D1 receptors (atypicals also block GABA-A)
The key target is D2.
Block dopamine reuptake (atypicals also block serotonin reuptake)
They block D2 receptors.
se: Weight gain and metabolic syndrome (olanzapine, clozapine)
items.sewhy: D2 blockade in the basal ganglia causes extrapyramidal effects and in the pituitary raises prolactin; H1, muscarinic and α1 effects cause sedation and weight gain; clozapine adds agranulocytosis and myocarditis.

ci.c: Dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson's disease
ci.why: Severe neuroleptic sensitivity: rigidity, falls, death
x: Mild sedation only: safe at normal doses
People with DLB can have severe, even fatal, sensitivity.
Not worse psychosis; severe rigidity, falls and death.

ci.c: Long QT or recent MI (especially haloperidol)
x: Myocarditis is a clozapine risk; here it's torsades.
No; NMS recurrence can be fatal.
No; NMS can recur and be fatal.

ci.why: ↑ stroke and death: lowest dose, review at 6 weeks
x: They raise stroke and death risk; use the lowest dose and review at 6 weeks.
↑ stroke and death: double the dose, review at 6 months
The risk is stroke and death; review rather than stopping abruptly.

items.name: Benzodiazepines
items.how: Enhance GABA-A receptor (↑ Cl⁻ channel opening frequency)
hx: Enhance GABA-A receptor (↑ Cl⁻ channel opening duration)
Longer opening is barbiturates; benzodiazepines increase opening frequency.
Block GABA-A receptor (↓ Cl⁻ channel opening)
They enhance GABA-A.
Activate GABA-B receptor (↑ K⁺ efflux)
That's baclofen; benzodiazepines act on GABA-A.
items.sewhy: Enhancing GABA depresses the CNS (drowsiness, falls, respiratory depression, especially with opioids or alcohol); receptors adapt, so dependence develops and abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures.

ci.c: Respiratory depression or type 2 respiratory failure

x: They precipitate encephalopathy; lorazepam (no active metabolites) is safer.
Diazepam has long-acting metabolites; lorazepam is safer.
The main danger is respiratory depression.

items.name: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors

uses.t: Dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson's dementia

hx: ↓ synaptic acetylcholine
They block its breakdown, raising synaptic ACh.
↑ synaptic dopamine
No; acetylcholine.
↑ synaptic GABA
No; acetylcholine.
items.sewhy: More acetylcholine in the gut (nausea, diarrhoea), at the heart's SA and AV nodes (bradycardia, heart block, syncope) and in the bladder (incontinence).

ci.c: Sick sinus syndrome, heart block, bradycardia
x: More ACh raises vagal tone, slowing the heart.
No; ↑ vagal tone → bradycardia and syncope.

items.name: Memantine
hx: NMDA receptor agonist (↑ glutamate signalling)
It blocks NMDA receptors.
GABA-B agonist (↓ glutamate release)
It's an NMDA antagonist.
Dopamine agonist (↑ frontal dopamine)
It's an NMDA antagonist.
items.sewhy: Partial NMDA blockade is well tolerated; dizziness, headache, constipation and raised BP are the main effects.

x: No; it may lower the seizure threshold.

items.name: Triptans
hx: 5-HT1B/1D antagonist → cranial vasodilation, ↑ CGRP release
They're agonists: cranial vasoconstriction and less CGRP.
CGRP receptor antibody → blocks cranial vasodilation
That's a migraine preventer (e.g. erenumab); triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists.
Ergot alkaloid → generalised vasoconstriction
Triptans are selective 5-HT1B/1D agonists, not ergots.
items.sewhy: 5-HT1B/1D agonism constricts cranial and, to a lesser extent, coronary vessels (chest tightness), and causes tingling and flushing; avoid in coronary disease.

ci.c: Ischaemic heart disease, coronary vasospasm, previous MI

x: They raise BP; vasoconstriction causes ischaemia.

items.name: Sodium valproate
items.how: ↑ GABA, blocks Na⁺ and T-type Ca²⁺ channels
hx: ↓ GABA, opens Na⁺ and L-type Ca²⁺ channels
It boosts GABA and blocks Na⁺ and T-type Ca²⁺ channels.
Enhances glycine receptors in the spinal cord
It raises GABA and blocks Na⁺ and T-type Ca²⁺ channels.
↑ glutamate, blocks K⁺ channels
It increases GABA, not glutamate.
items.sewhy: Valproate causes weight gain, tremor and hair thinning; it can cause idiosyncratic liver failure and pancreatitis, low platelets, and it's highly teratogenic.

ci.c: Women and girls who could become pregnant (unless on Pregnancy Prevention Programme)
ci.why: ~10% major malformations (neural tube defects) and ~30–40% neurodevelopmental problems
x: ~1% minor malformations (skin tags) and no neurodevelopmental effects
Valproate is highly teratogenic: ~10% malformations and 30–40% neurodevelopmental problems.
~10% major malformations (cardiac only) and no neurodevelopmental effects
Neural tube defects are typical, and 30–40% have neurodevelopmental problems.
~50% miscarriage, but no malformations in survivors
The main risks are malformations and neurodevelopmental problems.

items.name: Carbamazepine
hx: Opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
It blocks them.
Blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels
That's ethosuximide; carbamazepine blocks Na⁺ channels.
Blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels
It blocks Na⁺ channels.
items.sewhy: It enhances ADH action (SIADH, low sodium), causes HLA-linked severe skin reactions (SJS/TEN), affects the cerebellum and vestibular system (diplopia, ataxia), and induces liver enzymes.

ci.why: High risk of SJS/TEN: test first
x: High risk of liver failure: test first
High risk of agranulocytosis: check the FBC first
Low risk of side effects: no test needed
Carbamazepine can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures.
Carbamazepine induces enzymes, reducing their effect.
No; enzyme induction reduces their effect.

items.name: Lamotrigine and levetiracetam

items.how: Lamotrigine: Na⁺ channel block; levetiracetam: SV2A binding
hx: Lamotrigine: SV2A binding; levetiracetam: Na⁺ channel block
Swapped: lamotrigine blocks Na⁺ channels; levetiracetam binds SV2A.
Lamotrigine: GABA-A enhancement; levetiracetam: T-type Ca²⁺ block
Lamotrigine blocks Na⁺ channels; levetiracetam binds SV2A.
Lamotrigine: carbonic anhydrase inhibition; levetiracetam: NMDA antagonism
Lamotrigine: Na⁺ channels; levetiracetam: SV2A.
items.sewhy: Lamotrigine can cause serious rashes (SJS), especially with fast dose increases or valproate; levetiracetam commonly causes irritability and low mood.

ci.why: Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels → rash risk
x: Valproate inhibits its metabolism, doubling levels.
Lamotrigine doubles valproate levels → liver failure
Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels → kidney stones

items.name: Phenytoin
items.how: Blocks Na⁺ channels; zero-order kinetics at therapeutic levels
hx: Blocks Na⁺ channels; first-order kinetics at therapeutic levels
Its metabolism saturates, so kinetics turn zero-order: small dose rises cause big level jumps.
Opens Cl⁻ channels; first-order kinetics
It blocks Na⁺ channels, with zero-order kinetics.
Blocks Ca²⁺ channels; zero-order kinetics only in overdose
Na⁺ channel block, and zero-order within the therapeutic range.
items.sewhy: Phenytoin stimulates fibroblasts (gum overgrowth, coarse features, hirsutism), causes cerebellar signs when levels rise (zero-order kinetics) and is teratogenic; IV, it depresses the heart.

items.name: Levodopa
items.how: Dopamine precursor; carbidopa/benserazide stop peripheral breakdown
hx: Dopamine agonist; carbidopa/benserazide boost central breakdown
It's a precursor; the add-ons stop peripheral conversion.
Dopamine precursor; carbidopa/benserazide stop central breakdown
They act peripherally (they don't cross the BBB).
MAO-B inhibitor; carbidopa/benserazide block COMT
Levodopa is a dopamine precursor; carbidopa blocks peripheral dopa decarboxylase.
items.sewhy: Dopamine outside the brain causes nausea and postural hypotension; fluctuating levels cause dyskinesia and on–off swings; excess dopamine in limbic areas causes hallucinations.

x: MAOIs stop dopamine and NA breakdown → hypertensive crisis.

ci.why: Severe rigidity and hyperthermia (like NMS); time-critical medicine
x: Rebound dyskinesia; safe to miss a few doses
Missed doses risk rigidity and hyperthermia; give on time.
Severe hypotension; restart at half dose
The risk is NMS-like rigidity and hyperthermia.

items.name: Gabapentinoids
items.how: Bind α2δ subunit of Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ excitatory neurotransmitter release
hx: Bind GABA-A receptors → ↑ inhibitory signalling
Despite the name, they don't act on GABA receptors; they bind α2δ.
Bind α2δ subunit of Na⁺ channels → ↑ excitatory neurotransmitter release
α2δ belongs to Ca²⁺ channels, and release falls.
Block substance P (NK1) receptors → ↓ pain signalling
They bind the α2δ subunit of Ca²⁺ channels.
items.sewhy: They reduce neuronal calcium entry, depressing the CNS (dizziness, drowsiness) and adding to opioid respiratory depression; they're misused, so they're controlled drugs.

x: The concern is misuse (they're controlled drugs).
Not the key reason; misuse potential.

items.name: Topiramate
items.how: Na⁺ channel block, ↑ GABA, AMPA antagonism, carbonic anhydrase inhibition
hx: Na⁺ channel opening, ↓ GABA, AMPA agonism, carbonic anhydrase activation

SV2A binding, D2 blockade, NMDA agonism
Topiramate: Na⁺ block, ↑ GABA, AMPA antagonism, carbonic anhydrase inhibition.

items.sewhy: Topiramate inhibits carbonic anhydrase (paraesthesia, kidney stones), slows cognition and suppresses appetite; it can cause acute angle closure by swelling the ciliary body.

ci.c: Pregnancy, or could become pregnant without effective contraception
x: Topiramate is linked to cleft lip/palate and low birthweight.
No; cleft lip/palate and low birthweight.
No; carbonic anhydrase inhibition (alkaline urine, low citrate).

ci.why: Reduces contraceptive effect at higher doses
x: Increases contraceptive effect at higher doses
